title_prefix: The whole wallet database is materialize
mechanism: Core's walletdb loader never holds more than one record: LoadRecords (refs/bitcoin/src/wallet/walletdb.cpp:471-506) opens a PREFIX cursor per record type and streams rows through a per-type load function, so peak memory is one key/value pair and record types the caller did not ask for are never read. Its backup is the same shape a level lower: SQLiteDatabase::Backup (refs/bitcoin/src/wallet/sqlite.cpp:344-360) is sqlite3_backup_init/step, a page copy inside SQLite with no application-side buffer. Ours materializes the whole database twice over. wallet-db-records (src/wallet/wallet-store.lisp:429-445) pushes every (key . value) pair of a full iterator scan onto one list; %load-wallet-records (src/wallet/wallet.lisp:1047-1056) binds that list and walks it twice; and %wallet-dump-lines (src/wallet/wallet-crypt.lisp:640-650) calls the same function and MAPCARs it into a list of hex strings, which %write-wallet-dump (:651-696) then concatenates into a single with-output-to-string body before writing anything.
consequence: No wrong answer, and the signalling behaviour on a truncated scan (leveldb-iter-check-error at wallet-store.lisp:443) is deliberately safer than a silent short read -- but peak heap on loadwallet and backupwallet scales with the whole wallet file instead of being constant, and the multiplier on the backup path is large because the dump is hex (2 characters per byte) held whole in a Lisp string (4 bytes per character on SBCL) on top of the record list. Measured at 50,000 tx-shaped records of 400 bytes (20 MB of values): load retains about 30 MiB live where the streaming shape retains one pair, and the backup peaks near 500 MiB above baseline for the same 20 MB database, roughly 25x the file. A real wallet with a large transaction history therefore turns backupwallet into a multi-hundred-megabyte transient allocation, and on a memory-constrained node a backup can fail or provoke a GC pause where Core's page copy costs nothing. Load is the milder half, since Core also keeps every CWalletTx in mapWallet; the divergence there is only the extra raw copy.
evidence: Container /Users/sen/common-lisp/bl-ga11v-misc-s3d, warm image, probe-c.lisp, 50,000 records x 400-byte values in a fresh wallet LevelDB, sb-ext:get-bytes-consed and sb-kernel:dynamic-usage around each shape, full GC between them. Output: (:STREAMING-SCAN :MS 11 :MIB-CONSED 23 :RESULT (50000 20000000)) (:WALLET-DB-RECORDS :MS 14 :MIB-CONSED 30 :RESULT (50000 164)) (:HEAP-MIB-AFTER-RELEASE 134) (:BACKUP-DUMP-BODY :MS 108 :MIB-CONSED 612 :RESULT (:CHARS 43600000 :HEAP-MIB 629)). Reading them: the streaming scan conses 23 MiB but retains none of it; wallet-db-records leaves the heap at 164 MiB with the list live against 134 MiB once released, i.e. about 30 MiB retained for a 20 MB database; the dump body is a single 43.6-million-character string and drives the heap to 629 MiB, about 495 MiB above the same baseline. Time is not the problem (14 ms vs 11 ms for the load scan); memory is. Ours: src/wallet/wallet-store.lisp:429-445, src/wallet/wallet.lisp:1047-1056, src/wallet/wallet-crypt.lisp:640-696. Core: refs/bitcoin/src/wallet/walletdb.cpp:471-506, refs/bitcoin/src/wallet/sqlite.cpp:344-360.
fix_shape: Turn wallet-db-records into a driver rather than a collector: keep the iterator and the leveldb-iter-check-error guarantee, but hand each (key . value) to a callback (a with-wallet-db-records macro over the existing with-leveldb-iterator) so no caller has to hold the set. The backup path converts directly -- %write-wallet-dump should stream each hex line into the open temp file and feed the running hash256 incrementally instead of building a body string, which removes both the record list and the 4-bytes-per-character buffer and makes the checksum a single pass. The load path needs one more step because it is genuinely two-pass (descriptors before keys and caches, tx records last): either iterate the database once per pass, which is what Core's per-type prefix cursors amount to and is cheap because LevelDB keys are already type-prefixed, or seek to each type's prefix the way GetNewPrefixCursor does. Do not weaken the truncated-scan check in either case. The cost assertion in any regression test needs a positive control -- measure the old shape in the same run -- or a memory ceiling will pass vacuously.
